newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia opposition protests against Milosevic again.
newsitem.headline: Serbia opposition protests against Milosevic again.

text.p: Tens of thousands of protesters marched in pouring rain in Belgrade on Tuesday, demanding Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic concede defeat in local elections and accusing his ruling Socialists of poll fraud.
Serbian opposition leaders said their protests against the authorities' annulment of November 17 voting were picking up steam and had turned into a referendum on Milosevic himself.
Opposition marchers hurled abuse at the state television station -- a symbol of Milosevic's authoritarian rule.
The demonstrators, including children and pensioners, pelted the building with eggs and some threw stones, shattering windows on the ground floor.
Authorities have brought in hundreds of police with riot gear but so far officers have kept a low profile and the protests have remained peaceful.

The Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition has led Serbia's biggest demonstrations in five years after accusing authorities of stealing their shock victories in run-off local elections, including for the Belgrade city council.
Zajedno says the Socialist party made a mockery of the democratic process by annulling the results on the pretext of unspecified irregularities.
Zoran Djindjic, who has emerged as the dominant figure in the opposition, told the crowd Zajedno wanted "all of Serbia and all the world to find out that a party dictatorship rules in this country".
Speaking from the fourth floor window of opposition headquarters, Vuk Draskovic, another Zajedno leader, said a week of protests had gained international attention.
"Finally we can hear the world's sympathies," said Draskovic. "It took us seven days to do this, for the voice and the will of the people to be heard."
Draskovic called on army officers to join the protests and alleged some police were opposed to Milosevic.
A demonstration drew an estimated 150,000 on Monday. Not since 1991 have so many taken to the streets against Milosevic, who crushed those protests with tanks.

Demonstrations were under way in other major towns and several thousand people attended an opposition rally in Montenegro, which together with Serbia comprises rump Yugoslavia, independent Belgrade radio B-92 reported.
Some 10,000 students from Belgrade university staged a march at midday, chanting against Milosevic.
Joined by at least 30 law professors, students halted traffic as they marched past foreign embassies and ministries.
They hurled eggs and a few stones at offices of the Yugoslav United Left, the party led by Milosevic's Marxist wife. The students said they planned sit-ins at five faculties.
The United States has condemned the annulment of the municipal election results, which had shown victories for the Zajedno coalition in 15 of the country's 18 biggest towns.

Charges that authorities committed massive fraud prompted the European Union on Monday to postpone giving the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro preferential trade status granted to other countries in the region.

Electoral commissions and courts last week annulled poll results in almost all towns where Zajedno claimed victory. In Belgrade, a court on Sunday stripped Zajedno of a majority in the city council which authorities had earlier confirmed.
Electoral commissions have called for another round of voting on Wednesday and Sunday.
Zajedno has urged a boycott of the third round in the capital. Opposition leaders in some towns said they would run in the third round despite their objections.
Strong international support is considered crucial for the opposition but Zajedno officials said privately they had received no promises from the West.

The United States and European powers once accused Milosevic of igniting war in the former Yugoslavia. They now view him as a pillar of Balkan peace after he signed the Dayton treaty for Bosnia last year.
Zajedno leaders argue that they too are committed to the Dayton accords and that they advocate democratic reforms in Serbia which would bring stability to the region.
